The Tip Behind Netanyahu’s Stolen-Election Warning

On Election Day, Benjamin Netanyahu pointed to the arrests of three Ra’am activists and warned voters, “They are trying to steal the elections from us.” He did not mention that his own chief of staff and a former aide had helped set the arrests in motion, The New York Times reports.

Police said they suspected a plot to bribe voters and had seized envelopes of cash. Ra’am denied the allegation. Police later acknowledged in court that they had searched at least two homes without warrants. All three men were released without charge.

The judge who ordered one activist’s release noted that the file showed him campaigning for Ra’am and taking part in meetings with candidates. “But that’s not a crime,” the judge added.

Netanyahu’s office initially denied reports that police acted on a tip from chief of staff Ido Norden. After a Channel 12 investigation, the office acknowledged that Norden had passed along information and said he had acted “like any other citizen.”

A lawyer for former Netanyahu aide Daniel Greenberg confirmed his client was the source of the tip and denied that he had tried to improperly influence the vote. The attorney general and state prosecutor are looking into the matter.

Arab-led parties won a record 19 of the Knesset’s 120 seats. Election officials say there is no proof of widespread fraud that could have affected the result.

Whether anyone improperly influenced the police is still an open question. What is already on the record is how the arrests were used. Netanyahu’s chief of staff passed the tip to police, and Netanyahu presented the arrests as evidence that others were trying to steal the vote.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
